definition: The smallest structural and functional unit of life; every living organism is made of one or more cells.
The membrane-bound organelle in eukaryotic cells that stores DNA and controls the cell's activities.
The 'powerhouse of the cell' — an organelle that breaks down glucose with oxygen to release usable energy (ATP).
A selectively permeable barrier made of a phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves the cell.
The cell structure where amino acids are linked together to build proteins, following mRNA instructions.
Deoxyribonucleic acid — a double-stranded molecule made of A, T, G, C bases that stores an organism's hereditary instructions.
Ribonucleic acid — usually single-stranded, uses the base Uracil instead of Thymine, and helps carry out DNA's instructions.
The basic building block of DNA/RNA: a sugar, a phosphate group, and one nitrogenous base joined together.
In DNA, Adenine always pairs with Thymine (A-T) and Guanine always pairs with Cytosine (G-C), held by hydrogen bonds.
The twisted-ladder, two-strand 3D shape of DNA discovered by Watson and Crick in 1953, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data.
The flow of genetic information in cells: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.
The process of copying a DNA gene's sequence into a complementary messenger RNA (mRNA) strand, inside the nucleus.
The process where a ribosome reads mRNA codons and assembles the matching amino acids into a protein chain.
A set of three mRNA bases that codes for one specific amino acid (or a start/stop signal) during translation.
A segment of DNA that contains the instructions to make one protein or functional RNA molecule.
One of two or more alternative versions of a gene that can exist at the same position (locus) on a chromosome.
A trait that is expressed in an organism's appearance whenever at least one copy of its allele is present.
A trait that is only expressed when both inherited alleles for that gene are the recessive version.
The actual pair of alleles an organism carries for a trait (e.g., Tt), as opposed to how the trait looks.
The observable physical or biochemical characteristic produced by an organism's genotype (e.g., tall plant).
The stage of development when reproductive organs mature and secondary sexual characteristics appear.
The fusion of a sperm cell and an egg cell (ovum) to form a single-celled zygote, starting a new organism.
The single diploid cell formed immediately after fertilization, which divides repeatedly to form an embryo.
The organ that connects a developing fetus to the uterine wall, exchanging nutrients, oxygen, and waste.
The roughly 28-day hormonal cycle that prepares the uterus for a possible pregnancy each month.
Darwin's idea that organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully.
An inherited trait that improves an organism's chance of survival and reproduction in its environment.
The evolutionary process by which populations evolve to become distinct, separate species over time.
The preserved remains or traces of an ancient organism, used as evidence for how life has changed over time.
Body parts that are structurally similar across species because they evolved from a shared ancestor (e.g., human arm, bat wing).
A community of living organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living (physical) environment.
A straight-line sequence showing how energy and nutrients move from producers to a series of consumers.
An organism, usually a green plant or alga, that makes its own food using sunlight through photosynthesis.
An organism such as a fungus or bacterium that breaks down dead matter, recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem.
The variety of life — species, genes, and ecosystems — found in a particular habitat or across the planet.
The use of living organisms, cells, or their molecules to develop useful products and technologies.
DNA formed by artificially joining DNA fragments from two different sources, often used to insert a useful gene.
Polymerase Chain Reaction — a lab technique that makes millions of copies of a specific DNA segment quickly.
A precise gene-editing tool that uses a guide RNA and the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at an exact target location.
A lab method that separates DNA or protein fragments by size using an electric current through a gel.
A microorganism, such as a bacterium, virus, or fungus, that can cause disease in a host organism.
A Y-shaped protein made by the immune system that recognizes and helps neutralize a specific antigen.
A preparation that trains the immune system to recognize a pathogen safely, without causing the actual disease.
A tiny infectious particle that cannot reproduce on its own and must hijack a host cell's machinery to copy itself.
When bacteria evolve so that antibiotics no longer effectively kill them, often due to overuse of antibiotics.
Basic Local Alignment Search Tool — software that finds regions of similarity between a query sequence and a database.
A simple text format for representing a DNA, RNA, or protein sequence, starting with a '>' header line.
Arranging two or more DNA/protein sequences to identify regions of similarity that may show shared ancestry or function.
National Center for Biotechnology Information — a public US database and toolset for DNA, protein, and literature data.
An AI system by DeepMind that predicts a protein's 3D structure directly from its amino acid sequence with high accuracy.
